[1] In 1934 the publisher Allen Lane spent a weekend in Devon with the novelist Agatha Christie. Waiting at Exeter station for the train back to London, he searched the bookstall for something to read and found only glossy magazines and reprints of forgettable novels. Good books existed, of course, but in Britain a new hardback cost about seven shillings. That was well beyond what most travelers would invest on a few hours of reading.

[2] Lane's answer was simple. He would sell good books, novels and biographies that had already succeeded in hardback, for sixpence each, roughly the price of a pack of cigarettes. Other publishers thought the plan was generous. If serious books cost so little, they argued, readers would stop buying the expensive editions, and authors would earn almost nothing.

[3] Lane went ahead anyway. The first ten Penguins appeared in the summer of 1935 their covers divided into three horizontal bands: orange for fiction, green for crime, and blue for biography. The design was plain, it was also easy to recognize from across a shop. Lane did not wait for bookshops to come around. Instead, he persuaded the chain store Woolworths to place a large order, and the books were soon stacked beside the kitchenware and the sweets.

[4] The gamble paid off. Sales of the first ten titles was strong enough that Penguin sold three million books within a year, and rival publishers who had predicted ruin began launching cheap series of their own. During the Second World War, special editions went to the armed forces. Printed in special editions small enough for a uniform pocket, soldiers carried paperbacks from camp to camp and passed them along until the pages came loose.

[5] Penguin's success did more than make a fortune for one publisher. It changed who could own a library. Clerks and factory workers could now buy a novel every week out of their spare change and keep it on a shelf at home. Ninety years later, the bookstall that disappointed Lane is long gone, but the idea he had there is on sale in stations around the world.
prompt: In paragraph 3, in the sentence "Instead, he persuaded the chain store Woolworths to place a large order, and the books were soon stacked beside the kitchenware and the sweets." which choice provides the most logical transition in place of "Instead,"?
explanation: The preceding sentence says Lane did not wait for bookshops; this sentence says what he did in place of waiting. "Instead," marks that replacement. "Likewise" would claim the order resembled the waiting, "Even so" would set the order against something it does not contradict, and "Otherwise" would describe what happens if he does not act.

passage:
[1] A common octopus resting on a reef can vanish in less than a second. Its skin shifts from rusty red to the mottled gray-green of the rock beneath it, and small bumps rise on its surface to mock the texture of algae. Few animals can change their appearance so completely or so quickly.

[2] The trick begins with cells called chromatophores. Each one is a tiny elastic sac of pigment—yellow, red, brown, or black, ringed by muscles. When the muscles contract, they stretch the sac wide, and the pigment spreads across a larger patch of skin. When the muscles relax, the sac shrinks back to a dot that is almost invisible. Because each of these muscles are wired to nerves from the brain, an octopus can open thousands of sacs at once.

[3] Beneath the chromatophores lies two other layers of cells. Iridophores reflect light to produce shimmering blues and greens, and leucophores scatter all colors equally, giving the skin a bright white background. Working together, the three layers allow an octopus to produce an enormous range of patterns, from stripes and spots to flickering bands of color.

[4] What puzzles biologists is that the octopus appears to be colorblind. Its eyes contain only one type of light-sensitive pigment, which should let it see brightness but not hue. Similarly, it matches the color of its surroundings with remarkable accuracy.

[5] Researchers have proposed two explanations, and they are not mutually exclusive. One is that the skin itself can sense light: proteins similar to those in the eye have been found in octopus skin. The other concerns the animal's oddly shaped pupil, which may bring different colors into focus at slightly different distances and so give the brain clues about hue. Neither idea has yet been proven, the octopus's disappearing act remains, at least in part, a mystery.
prompt: In paragraph 2, in the sentence "Because each of these muscles are wired to nerves from the brain, an octopus can open thousands of sacs at once." which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "are wired"?
explanation: The subject is "each," which is singular; "of these muscles" only describes it. The verb must be singular and present, like the rest of the paragraph: "is wired." "Are," "were," and "have been" are all plural forms.

passage:
[1] The summer I turned sixteen, I took a job at Delgado Hardware a narrow shop wedged between a laundromat and a shoe-repair stand. On my first morning, Mr. Delgado handed me a canvas apron and pointed at the key-cutting machine in the back corner. "That," he said, "is the most important machine in the store."

[2] I thought he was joking. The machine looked like a greasy vise bolted to a grinding wheel, and it accomplished only one feat. A customer handed me a key; I clamped it beside a blank, and a metal guide traced the old key's ridges while the wheel cut the same shape into the new one. The whole process took about forty seconds.

[3] For the first week I cut keys badly. Some came out with burrs so sharp they snagged the lining of a pocket, and others turned stiffly in the lock or not at all. Mr. Delgado never scolds me. Therefore, he would take each failed key, run his thumb along its edge, and hand it back without a word, and I would try again.

[4] By August I had cut hundreds of keys, and I had started to notice who needed them. A woman whose husband had just moved out wanted three copies, one for each of her children. A college student bought a key to his first apartment and held it up to the light as if it were a medal. An elderly man asked for a spare because he kept locking himself out, and he laughed about it, but his hands shook as he paid.

[5] On my last day Mr. Delgado asked me whether I finally understood about the machine. I told him I did. A key, I had learned, rarely just a piece of metal. It is usually a sign that something in someone's life is beginning, ending, or getting harder to manage, and for forty seconds at a time I had been part of it.
prompt: In paragraph 3, in the sentence "Therefore, he would take each failed key, run his thumb along its edge, and hand it back without a word, and I would try again." which choice provides the most logical transition in place of "Therefore,"?
explanation: The preceding sentence says what Mr. Delgado did not do (scold); this sentence says what he did in its place. "Instead," marks that substitution. "Therefore" makes the silent handing-back a result of not scolding, and "Likewise" and "Moreover" add the gesture as a further item of the same kind.

[1] Walk across almost any college campus and you will find them: narrow strips of bare dirt cutting diagonally across the lawns. Planners call these trails "desire lines" or "desire paths." No one designs them. They appear because hundreds of people, each acting alone, decide that the paved walkway takes too long and step onto the grass. The next person sees the flattened strip and follows it.

[2] [A] For decades, the usual response was to fight them. Groundskeepers put up fences, planted hedges, and posted signs asking people to stay on the walkways. [B] As a result, these measures rarely worked for long. [C] A fence would be stepped over and a hedge trampled. [D] Within a season the dirt line would return, often in exactly the same place.

[3] Some planners have taken the identical approach. Rather than deciding in advance where people should walk, they wait to see where people actually do. At a few universities, new lawns have been left unpaved for a year after construction. Once the desire paths have formed, workers pave them the result is a network of walkways that matches how the campus is really used.

[4] The idea has spread beyond campuses. City officials in several countries has studied desire paths in parks and around transit stations, treating each worn trail as a kind of vote for a route that no one planned. A path that cuts behind a bus shelter for instance, may reveal that the official crossing is too far from the stop.

[5] Desire paths are not always a sign of poor design. Sometimes a shortcut damages tree roots or crossing a slope that erodes easily, and a barrier is the right answer. But planners who read them carefully have learned something useful. The people who use a space every day often know it better than the people who drew it.
prompt: This question asks about the essay as a whole. Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to argue that cities should stop building paved walkways until people have chosen their own routes. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?
choices: Yes, because it presents worn trails as votes for routes that city officials failed to plan.
No, because it argues that fences and hedges remain the most reliable way to protect a lawn.
No, because it presents waiting to pave as one practice and grants that barriers are sometimes right.
Yes, because it reports that some universities leave new lawns unpaved for a year before paving the trails that form.
correct_answer: No, because it presents waiting to pave as one practice and grants that barriers are sometimes right.
explanation: The essay reports what some planners do and ends by granting that desire paths are not always a sign of poor design; it never calls for cities to stop paving. The year-long wait happens only "at a few universities," the vote image explains what officials learn, and the essay says fences and hedges rarely worked.

passage:
[1] In the summer of 1858, London baked under some of the hottest weather anyone could remember, and the River Thames began to stink. For centuries the city had emptied its waste into the river, and by the 1850s, when the city had more than two million residents, the Thames was little more than an open sewer. As the water warmed, the smell grew so powerful that newspapers called it the Great Stink.

[2] The stench reached even the Houses of Parliament, which stand on the riverbank. Workers hung curtains soaked in chemicals over the windows, but lawmakers still fled the committee rooms with handkerchiefs pressed to their faces. Within weeks, Parliament approves a plan it has been putting off for years.

[3] The plan belonged to Joseph Bazalgette, chief engineer of the citys' Metropolitan Board of Works. He proposed a network of large brick sewers running alongside the Thames that would catch the waste before it reached the river and carry it miles to the east, where it could be liberated on the outgoing tide. Bazalgette, whom colleagues knew for his caution, worked out how wide each pipe needed to be and then doubled the figure, reasoning that the job would be done only once.

[4] Most Londoners of the time believed that diseases such as cholera spread through foul air, and Bazalgette's sewers were built to remove a smell. For example, they had an effect that no one had planned. Waste no longer flowed into the river where much of the city drew its drinking water from, and cholera, which had killed tens of thousands of Londoners in earlier outbreaks, largely disappeared. The last major outbreak, in 1866, struck a district that had not yet been connected to the new system.

[5] Much of Bazalgette's network is still in use, in recent years London has built a new tunnel beneath the Thames to handle the overflow from a city far larger than the one he planned for.
prompt: In paragraph 3, in the sentence "He proposed a network of large brick sewers running alongside the Thames that would catch the waste before it reached the river and carry it miles to the east, where it could be liberated on the outgoing tide." which choice is most precise in context in place of "liberated"?
explanation: Waste let out into the river on the tide is simply "released." "Liberated" and "emancipated" mean freed from captivity or oppression, and "acquitted" means declared not guilty; each treats sewage as if it were a person.

[1] On December 21, 1913, readers of the New York World found something new in the paper's Sunday supplement: a diamond-shaped grid of empty squares with a list of numbered clues beneath it. Its creator, a Liverpool-born journalist named Arthur Wynne, called it a "Word-Cross." Within a few weeks, a typesetting mix-up had reversed the name, and the puzzle has been a crossword ever since.

[2] For a decade, a period of ten years, the World was nearly the only paper to print one. Then, in 1924, a young publishing firm called Simon & Schuster released a book of crosswords; its first title. The book sold hundreds of thousands of copies, and a craze followed. Bands recorded songs about crosswords, and one railroad reportedly placed dictionaries in its passenger cars for puzzling travelers. Dictionaries flew off store shelves, and libraries complained that puzzle solvers were sharing their reference books.

[3] Not everyone was charmed. For example, the New York Times dismissed the crossword as a "sinful waste" of time. The paper eventually changed its mind, in 1942 it began running a Sunday puzzle, edited by a woman named Margaret Farrar. She would hold the job for more than twenty-five years.

[4] Farrar shaped the crossword more than anyone since Wynne. She required symmetrical grids, words of at least three letters, and for clues to be fair as well as clever. Her rules, along with her habit of testing every clue on a second solver, is still followed by most American puzzle editors.

[5] A century after Wynne's diamond, the crossword appears in hundreds of newspapers and on millions of phones. Its basic appeal has changed little since 1913. A good clue misleads without lying: "Bark," for instance, may point to a dog or to a tree. The pleasure of solving lies in the moment when a clue that seemed impossible suddenly makes sense.
prompt: In paragraph 3, in the sentence "The paper eventually changed its mind, in 1942 it began running a Sunday puzzle, edited by a woman named Margaret Farrar." which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "mind, in 1942 it"?
explanation: "The paper eventually changed its mind" and "in 1942 it began running a Sunday puzzle" are independent clauses. A semicolon joins them. The original is a comma splice, no punctuation fuses them, and adding a comma after "1942" leaves the comma splice in place.

passage:
[1] In the spring of certain years, the ground beneath the forests of the eastern United States begins to open. Small holes appear by the thousands, and one warm evening, as if on a signal, millions of insects crawl out of it at once. They are periodical cicadas, and they have spent the last thirteen or seventeen years underground.

[2] For nearly all of that time, a young cicada, called a nymph, lives in the dark, sucking sap from the roots of trees. It grows slowly, molting several times. How the nymphs keep count of the years are still not fully understood; some researchers think they track the yearly rise and fall of sap in the roots. When the time comes, the nymphs wait for the soil about eight inches down to warm to roughly 64 degrees Fahrenheit and then emerge.

[3] [A] Above ground, the adults have only a few weeks to live. [B] The males gather in the treetops and sing, producing a chorus loud enough to drown out conversation. [C] The females lie their eggs in slits that they cut into thin branches. [D] When the eggs hatch, the tiny nymphs drop to the ground and burrow down to begin the long wait again.

[4] Emerging all at once is itself an ambush. Birds, squirrels, and even dogs feast on the cicadas, but there are far more insects than predators can eat, so most survive long enough to breed. By contrast, an insect that emerged a week early or a year late would face the predators alone.

[5] The length of the cycle may matter too. Thirteen and seventeen are prime numbers, divisible only by themselves and one. Some biologists argue that a prime-numbered cycle makes it unlikely that cicadas will emerge in the same year as a predator whose numbers rise and fall on a shorter cycle. A brood on a twelve-year cycle would meet predators on two-, three-, four-, or six-year cycles every time it emerged, a thirteen-year brood would rarely meet any of them.
prompt: In paragraph 2, in the sentence "It grows slowly, molting several times." which choice is correctly punctuated in place of "slowly, molting"?
explanation: "Molting several times" is a participial phrase describing how the nymph grows, and a comma correctly attaches it to the clause. A semicolon or a period would leave the phrase standing alone as a fragment, and with no comma "slowly molting" reads as if the molting were slow.

passage:
[1] I was thirty-four the first time I put my face in the water on purpose. Growing up in a desert town, I had never learned to swim, and as an adult I had become expert at avoiding the subject. I stayed on the beach towel, offered to watch everyones' bags, and laughed when friends asked whether I was coming in.

[2] The adult class at the community pool met on Tuesday nights. There were six of us, a retired bus driver, two college students, a nurse, a man who had recently moved from Nepal, and me. The nurse had nearly drowned as a child; the bus driver simply wanted to keep up with his grandchildren. Our instructor, Paloma, was perhaps twenty years old and spoke to us with the urgency of someone talking a cat out of a tree.

[3] The first lesson had nothing to do with swimming. Paloma asked us to stand in the shallow end, take a breath, and lower our faces into the water while blowing bubbles through our noses. It sounds simple. For me it was terrifying, my body was convinced that the water would rush in and never leave.

[4] By the fourth week, I could float on my back if Paloma kept a hand under my shoulders. By the sixth, she took the hand away without telling me, and I floated on my own for nearly a minute before I noticed. When I realized what had happened, I panicked, swallowed half the pool, and came up coughing and laughing.

[5] I am still not a mighty swimmer. I swim slow, my kick is uneven, and I need to rest at the end of every length. But last summer, for the first time, I left the towel on the sand and walked into the lake with everyone else. Paloma would probably call that a passing grade.
prompt: In paragraph 4, in the sentence "When I realized what had happened, I panicked, swallowed half the pool, and came up coughing and laughing." which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "had happened"?
explanation: The floating happened before the narrator realized it, so the past perfect "had happened" is correct in this past-tense account. "Has happened" and "happens" shift into the present, and "would happen" points to something still to come.

[1] Our public library lends more than books. Since last spring, card holders have been able to borrow a pressure washer, a sewing machine, a telescope, or any of about two hundred other objects from the new "library of things" in the basement. The collection began with donations and a small grant, and it has been popular from the first week, the waiting list for the carpet cleaner is currently eleven names long.

[2] The county board will decide next month whether to give the program permanent funding. The vote is scheduled for the board's public meeting on the fourteenth. We urge it to say yes.

[3] The case is partly about money. Most households use a drill for a few minutes a year, and an infrequently used tool costs far more to own than to borrow. A family that borrows a tent for one camping trip save the cost of buying one and the space of storing it. Multiply those savings across a county of 90,000 people, and the program's extravagant budget looks like a bargain.

[4] The case is also about what a library is for. Libraries began as a way to share things that were too expensive for most people to own alone; in the nineteenth century, that meant books. Today a book is cheap, but a ladder long enough to reach a second-story gutter is not. Nevertheless, lending one fits the library's original purpose as well as lending a novel does.

[5] Critics argue that borrowed tools will come back broken. The library's records insinuate otherwise. Of more than 1,400 loans so far, staff have recorded less than twenty items returned damaged, and every one was repaired for less than the cost of a single new tool. The board should fund the program and let the waiting list for the carpet cleaner get shorter.
prompt: In paragraph 3, in the sentence "Multiply those savings across a county of 90,000 people, and the program's extravagant budget looks like a bargain." which choice best fits the context of the sentence in place of "extravagant"?
explanation: The editorial wants the budget funded and says it "looks like a bargain" next to the county's savings, so it describes the budget as small: "modest." "Extravagant," "lavish," and "bloated" all call the budget excessive, which would undercut the writers' own argument.

[1] The cliffs near Lyme Regis, on the southern coast of England, are made of soft gray rock and clay that crumble in winter storms. Each landslide exposes the remains of animals that lived in the sea some 200 million years ago. In the early 1800s, few people searched those cliffs as carefully, or as successfully, as Mary Anning.

[2] [A] Anning was born in 1799 into a poor family. [B] Her father, a cabinetmaker, collected fossils from the beach and sold them to tourists, and he often took his children along. [C] When he died in 1810, he left the family in debt, and fossil hunting became one of the ways the Anning's paid their bills. [D]

[3] Around 1811, Mary's brother Joseph found a strange skull in the cliffs. Over the following months, Mary, then about twelve, uncovered the rest of the skeleton; a creature with a long snout and paddle-like limbs that scientists later named Ichthyosaurus, or "fish lizard." In 1823 she found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, a marine reptile with a tiny head on an extraordinarily long neck. The find was so unusual as a leading French anatomist at first suspected it was a fake.

[4] Anning also noticed that certain stones found inside skeletons contains fish bones and scales, and she suggested that the stones were fossilized droppings. Scientists bought her specimens and drew on her observations, but they rarely named her when they published. As a woman, she was banished from the Geological Society of London; she could not even attend its meetings.

[5] Recognition came slowly. When she died in 1847, the society's president delivered a tribute to her, an unusual honor for someone who had never been allowed to join. Today several of her finds stand in the Natural History Museum in London, and the labels beside them carry her name.
prompt: This question asks about the essay as a whole. Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to show how a person without formal standing contributed to a science. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

No, because it reports that a leading anatomist believed one of her finds was a fake.
No, because it focuses on the debts that Anning's family faced after her father's death.
Yes, because it pairs Anning's discoveries with her exclusion from the Geological Society.
correct_answer: Yes, because it pairs Anning's discoveries with her exclusion from the Geological Society.
explanation: The essay describes the ichthyosaur, the plesiosaur, and Anning's idea about fossil droppings, and it stresses that she could not join or even attend the society. The cliffs' geology and the family's debts are background, and the anatomist's doubt is presented as a sign of how unusual her find was, not as proof that it was false.

[1] The Bayeux Tapestry is not, strictly speaking, a tapestry. A true tapestry is woven, with the design built into the fabric thread by thread. The Bayeux work was embroidered, its scenes were stitched in colored wool onto long strips of plain linen. The name stuck anyway, and after more than nine centuries no one seems inclined to change it.

[2] The embroidery is about half a meter tall and nearly seventy meters long. Scholars have counted more than six hundred human figures in its scenes, along with nearly two hundred horses and dozens of ships. It tells the story of the Norman conquest of England in 1066, from an oath that the English nobleman Harold supposedly swore to William, Duke of Normandy, to the Battle of Hastings, where Harold was killed. Short Latin captions names the people and places.

[3] Historians believe that the work was commissioned by William's half-brother, Bishop Odo, and it being probably made by English embroiderers within a few years of the battle. That origin makes it an ordinary document: a celebration of the Norman victory, stitched by people of the defeated nation.

[4] The main scenes are infested with detail. For instance, ships are loaded with wine barrels and horses, and soldiers wear shirts of chain mail. Above and below the story run two narrow borders filled with lions, birds, and scenes from fables. In one panel a comet streaks across the sky, a sight that observers in 1066 took as an omen, it is now thought to have been Halley's comet.

[5] The final section of the embroidery is missing, and no one knows how the story originally ended. Perhaps the last panels showed William's coronation. What survives, however, is remarkable enough. For anyone who wants to know how people in the eleventh century fought, dressed, and sailed, few sources are as vivid.
prompt: The writer is considering deleting the sentence "Perhaps the last panels showed William's coronation." from paragraph 5. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?
choices: Deleted, because it contradicts the statement in paragraph 2 that the story ends with the Battle of Hastings.
Kept, because it offers one possible answer to the question of how the story ended.
Kept, because it explains why the final section of the embroidery went missing.
Deleted, because paragraph 3 has already said that the work celebrates the Norman victory.
correct_answer: Kept, because it offers one possible answer to the question of how the story ended.
explanation: The preceding sentence says no one knows how the story originally ended, and "Perhaps" offers a guess. The sentence gives no reason for the loss; paragraph 2 describes the surviving story, which reaches Hastings, so a lost later scene does not contradict it; and a general remark about celebrating the victory does not make a specific guess redundant.

passage:
[1] Before 1883, nearly every town in the United States kept its own time. Noon was the moment the sun stood loftiest in the sky, and because the sun appears to move westward, noon in Boston came several minutes before noon in a town to its west. For most of history, this hardly mattered. In contrast, a farmer or a shopkeeper rarely needed to know what time it was two hundred miles away.

[2] The railroads changed that. A train leaving Chicago passed through dozens of local times on its way east, and each railroad kept their own schedule, usually set by the clock in its headquarters city. Stations sometimes displayed several clocks, one for each railroad that stopped there, and all of them were different. Travelers missed connections, and the risk of collisions on single-track lines were growing.

[3] The solution came not from the government but from the railroads themselves. At a meeting in 1883, railroad managers agreed to divide the country into four time zones, each one hour apart. Within each zone, every clock would show the same time.

[4] The change took effect at noon on November 18, 1883. In cities across the country, jewelers and telegraph operators reset their clocks as the signal arrived. Towns in the eastern part of each zone, set their clocks back and so experienced noon twice that day. Newspapers called it "the day of two noons."

[5] Not everyone was pleased. Some towns refused to give up "God's time," as they called solar time, and kept their old clocks for years. Yet within a generation, standard time had become so ordinary that most people forgot it had ever been an invention. Congress did not make the time zones law until 1918, by that time it was simply confirming what the country had been doing for thirty-five years.
prompt: In paragraph 5, in the sentence "Yet within a generation, standard time had become so ordinary that most people forgot it had ever been an invention." which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "had become"?
explanation: The sentence looks back from the point when people had forgotten to the change that came before it, so the past perfect "had become" is correct. "Has become" and "becomes" shift into the present, and "will have become" shifts into the future.
